sweep_summary: Eight title hits for Yucatec Maya (yuca1254; catalog: tonal, deciding source Kidder 2013 dissertation, open text held by the project). Only one item could be newly obtained and read: Kügler, Skopeteas & Verhoeven 2007 (ISIS 8, pp. 187-208), downloaded as the whole-volume PDF from the SFB 632 site and. it is an instrumental tone/information-structure study ('Yucatec Maya is a tone language, displaying a three-fold opposition'; long vowels obligatorily H or L, short vowels toneless; no intonational focus marking) and says nothing about word-stress placement, so it confirms the tonal coding and is silent on stress. Kidder's 2013 Benjamins chapter 'Stress in Yucatec Maya' is paywalled (Crossref abstract read: 'no detailed account of stress.. has been made'; the chapter is the Spanish-loanword diagnostic already contained in her open dissertation), priority low. McQuown 1975 'El acento del maya yucateco' (Lima, Instituto de Estudios Peruanos; pp. 59-71) is print-only (HathiTrust search-only, OCLC 7992974); Sobrino Gómez 2013 cites it among binary H/L tone analyses, so it is probably a tone statement; priority medium; Glottolog's 'Matos & Ravines 1975' is a duplicate record of the same paper under the volume editors' names. Uth 2018 and the two Michnowicz & Hyler 2020 chapters concern Yucatan Spanish prosody/rhythm (abstracts read via Crossref), and Redzich 2011 is medieval German philology (Glottolog mis-association) - all irrelevant to Maya word stress. The best first-hand stress statement read in this search of works with stress in the title is Andrade 1955 §1.6 (already held by the project from our reading of 9/16; re-read): accent lexically determined, dominant final accent in disyllables, penult accent when the penult has a long vowel, always-final in 4+ syllable words - the same shape as the Bricker et al. 1998 default that Kidder reviews; it refines the catalog's record of competing proposals but does not supersede Kidder 2013. Nothing found contradicts the 'tonal' coding. Benjamins, HathiTrust search, publishup and Bielefeld behind bot walls; web.archive.org unreachable.

new_statements.quote: Accent in Modern Yucatec appears to be determined lexically; with few exceptions, a sharp division can be made between those verbs in which the stem is accented, regardless of whether one, two, or more suffixes are added, and those whose stem is invariably unaccented. Regarding nouns, somewhat more complex behavior is noted. [...] (a) The most frequent pattern for disyllabic noun and verb forms is that in which the ultima bears the accent. [...] (b) The accent falls on the penult in a small number of nouns and verbs; and in all words which contain a double vowel in the penult. [...] In the relatively few words in the texts which contain more than three syllables, the ultima is invariably accented
new_statements.citation: Andrade, Manuel J. 1955. A Grammar of Modern Yucatec. Microfilm Collection of Manuscripts on Middle American Cultural Anthropology, Series 7, No. 41. University of Chicago Library (manuscript completed before 1941, released by N. A. McQuown); online edition by Christian Lehmann. Section 1.6 'Accent'.
new_statements.reading: The earliest first-hand descriptive account (1930s field texts): word accent is lexically fixed per stem, with final accent as the dominant disyllabic pattern, penult accent whenever the penult holds a long ('double') vowel, and invariable final accent in words of four or more syllables. In shape this is the same default that Bricker, Po'ot Yah & Dzul de Po'ot 1998 later state (stress the long vowel, otherwise the final syllable), but Andrade frames it as lexical with exceptions and notes that greater stress often accompanies lower pitch, i.e. stress is not identified with high tone. It adds a pre-Kidder first-hand data point on the 'stress is lexical/unpredictable' side of the debate the catalog already records; it does not overturn Kidder 2013's instrumental finding of no obligatory word-level stress pattern.

sources.quote: "Yucatec Maya is a tone language, displaying a three-fold opposition in the tonal realization of syllables." (p. 187) ... "lexical tone and intonation neither interact in the expression of topic nor of focus (Kügler & Skopeteas 2006)." (p. 188) ... "For syllables containing long vowels this tonal distinction is obligatory, whereas syllables containing short vowels are empty TBUs." (p. 196) ... "Yucatec Maya does not employ additional pitch accents to express topic or focus." (p. 196)
sources.locator: Abstract p. 187; sec. 1 p. 188; sec. 3.3 p. 196; sec. 3.4 pp. 196-197
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement. The paper is an instrumental study of lexical tone (H realized as a rise, L as low level; short vowels toneless) and of the absence of intonational focus marking; the strings 'stress'/'accent' occur only in the Bruce 1977 Swedish reference and in 'pitch accent' (intonation). It confirms the lexical-tone half of the catalog's classification and is silent on stress.

sources.quote: "Accents are generally not marked in Mayan and that may in part be due to the fact that in words of more than one syllable the accent often falls evenly on each one of the syllables. However, there are instances where there is a definite accent on either the first or the second sylable ... háan 'son-in-law' / haán 'filed'" (i.e. the long-vowel tone contrast described as 'accent'); "Tone plays an important part in spoken Mayan". Non-specialist grammar; no positional stress rule; not decisive.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian & Ryan Bennett. 2018 preprint (published 2020/2021). Mesoamerica. Ch. 27 in C. Gussenhoven & A. Chen (eds.), The Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody. Oxford: OUP.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: "There is little consensus over stress assignment in Yucatec. Since the influential early study of Pike (1946), Yucatec has been described as having some mix of quantity-sensitive and initial/final stress (e.g. Fisher 1973; Fox 1978; Bricker et al. 1998; Gussenhoven & Teeuw 2008...). Existing analyses are not all mutually compatible, and the actual phonetic cues to stress in Yucatec remain obscure. It has even been suggested that Yucatec, a tonal language..., may lack word-level stress altogether (Kidder 2013)." Tone: "Yucatec has a contrast between high /V́:/ and low /V̀:/ on long vowels".

sources.quote: "Though scholars have noted the existence of stress or accent since it was first documented centuries ago, no detailed account of stress as either a separate or related entity to tone or length has been made. In this paper, I analyze the phonetic changes evident in a series of loan words into YM from Spanish, a language without tone or length distinctions, found in elicited and conversational data as an initial step in diagnosing stress patterns in YM."
sources.note: Abstract only: no detailed account of YM stress exists; the chapter is the Spanish-loanword diagnostic (initial-syllable lengthening) that also forms part of Kidder's 2013 dissertation, which the catalog already holds in open text. Consistent with the catalog's 'no obligatory word-level stress pattern' reading.
